questions.stem: A student attempts to electrolyse solid sodium chloride using two electrodes and a battery. No products are formed at either electrode. Why does electrolysis fail with solid sodium chloride?

options.text: Sodium chloride does not contain ions
The ions in solid sodium chloride are held in fixed positions and cannot move to the electrodes
The battery does not provide enough voltage
Solid sodium chloride conducts electricity too well and short-circuits

questions.explanation: Solid ionic compounds contain ions, but these ions are locked in a rigid lattice structure and cannot move. For electrolysis to work, the ions must be free to move to the electrodes. This is why ionic compounds must be molten or dissolved in water for electrolysis to occur.

questions.stem: During electrolysis of molten lead bromide, lead forms at one electrode and bromine at the other. At which electrode does each product form?

options.text: Lead at the anode (positive electrode); bromine at the cathode (negative electrode)
Lead at the cathode (negative electrode); bromine at the anode (positive electrode)
Both form at the cathode
Lead at the anode; bromine at both electrodes

questions.explanation: Lead ions (Pb2+) are positive cations, so they are attracted to the negative electrode (cathode), where they gain electrons to form lead metal. Bromide ions (Br-) are negative anions, so they are attracted to the positive electrode (anode), where they lose electrons to form bromine. Opposite charges attract.

questions.stem: During electrolysis, cations move towards the cathode. What happens to the cations when they reach the cathode?

options.text: They lose electrons and are oxidised
They gain protons and become neutral
They gain electrons and are reduced to form atoms
They decompose into smaller ions

questions.explanation: At the cathode, positive metal ions (cations) gain electrons from the external circuit and are reduced to neutral metal atoms. For example, Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. Reduction always occurs at the cathode (remember: Reduction at the Cathode).

questions.stem: A student sets up electrolysis of a solution but forgets to add the electrolyte. The circuit contains only pure distilled water. What would happen?

options.text: Electrolysis would proceed normally, producing hydrogen and oxygen
Very little or no current would flow because pure water is a very poor conductor
The water would boil due to the electrical energy
The electrodes would dissolve into the water

questions.explanation: Pure distilled water contains very few free ions, so it is a very poor electrical conductor. Almost no current would flow through the circuit. An electrolyte (an ionic compound dissolved in water or molten) is needed to provide free-moving ions that carry the current and complete the circuit.

questions.stem: In electrolysis, why must the electrodes be connected to a direct current (DC) supply rather than alternating current (AC)?

options.text: AC would cause the electrolyte to heat up and evaporate
DC ensures ions move consistently to the correct electrodes; AC would reverse their direction constantly
AC cannot pass through liquids
DC is cheaper to produce than AC

questions.explanation: Direct current provides a constant positive and negative electrode, so cations always move to the cathode and anions always move to the anode. Alternating current reverses polarity many times per second, which would constantly change which electrode ions move towards, preventing consistent product formation at either electrode.
